title: Stereotactic Radiation for Vestibular Schwannomas and Meningiomas in NF2-Related Schwannomatosis: Treatment Selection and Long-Term Care
content: Treatment of vestibular schwannomas and meningiomas in NF2-related schwannomatosis (NF2-SWN) requires decisions about individual lesions in patients who may need repeated interventions. This structured narrative review examines how tumor behavior, neurological function, anatomy, previous treatment, and late risk inform stereotactic radiation. We used recent systematic reviews to identify the evidence base, supplemented by targeted MEDLINE/PubMed searches through 24 August 2026, citation tracking, and bibliographic verification. Most radiation evidence comes from retrospective single-fraction stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) cohorts. Selected vestibular schwannomas show durable control, but hearing preservation declines with follow-up. Meningioma control is generally high, while untreated lesions may progress and require further intervention. Hypofractionated stereotactic radiotherapy is an option when a therapeutic single-fraction plan cannot meet normal-tissue objectives; comparative superiority is unproven. Bevacizumab has prospective hearing-directed evidence for progressive vestibular schwannomas, and brigatinib has demonstrated multitumor activity. Their optimal sequence with local treatment remains undefined. Population-level evidence associates radiation exposure with later malignancy or malignant progression, although individual risk after contemporary SRS is uncertain. We translate these findings into a clinical-scenario matrix: establish the reason for intervention, identify any need for decompression or tissue, compare focal and systemic options, and document the functional objective and reassessment plan. This proposed framework is not a validated guideline. Its practical aim is to support treatment selection and follow-up without equating radiographic control with preserved hearing, vision, or independence.
